Genomic evaluation data: parameter estimation and cross-validation

Source: vignettes/articles/genomic-evaluation.Rmd
genomic-evaluation.Rmd

中文版

When genomic prediction models are compared, the usual questions are: is a multi-trait model more accurate than a single-trait model? Does adding another herd (population) to the reference population improve the prediction of this herd? What is the genetic correlation of a trait between two herds?

Each model needs two kinds of files:

  • parameter-estimation data: all records, to estimate variance components, heritabilities and genetic correlations;
  • cross-validation data: a training and a validation set for every repeat × fold, to compute prediction accuracy.

The four functions added in mintyr 0.2.3 turn this into three steps:

Step Function What it does
1 cv_folds() Assigns every individual to a fold within each group: one fold table
2 cv_scenarios() Builds parameter-estimation and CV data of five scenarios from that fold table
3 export_scenarios() Writes input files for ASReml, DMU, HIBLUP, … per scenario

apply_folds() is the building block behind cv_scenarios(); use it directly for custom designs (see Beyond the five scenarios).

library(mintyr)
library(data.table)

Example data

The examples use simulated data: two herds (north, south), three traits (adg, bf, fcr), the fixed effects sex and batch, and 400 SNP genotypes. Both herds share the same SNP effects, so adding the other herd to the reference population usually helps; adg and bf have a moderate genetic correlation; some phenotypes are missing.

set.seed(2026)
n_snp <- 400
n     <- c(north = 300, south = 280)
ids   <- c(sprintf("N%04d", seq_len(n[["north"]])), sprintf("S%04d", seq_len(n[["south"]])))

# Genotypes (0/1/2), from a SNP chip in practice; row names are the IDs
freq <- runif(n_snp, 0.05, 0.5)
geno <- sapply(freq, function(p) rbinom(length(ids), 2, p))
dimnames(geno) <- list(ids, paste0("snp", seq_len(n_snp)))
Z <- sweep(geno, 2, 2 * freq)                       # centred genotype matrix

# True breeding values, scaled to the heritability and phenotypic SD
bv <- function(b, h2, sd_p) { g <- drop(Z %*% b); g / sd(g) * sqrt(h2) * sd_p }
b_adg <- rnorm(n_snp)
b_bf  <- 0.5 * b_adg + sqrt(0.75) * rnorm(n_snp)   # genetic correlation with adg ~ 0.5
b_fcr <- rnorm(n_snp)

phe <- data.table(id = ids, herd = rep(names(n), n))
phe[, sex   := sample(c("M", "F"), .N, replace = TRUE)]
phe[, batch := paste0(herd, sample(2401:2404, .N, replace = TRUE))]
phe[, adg := round(900 + 20 * (sex == "M") + 30 * (herd == "south") +
                     bv(b_adg, 0.30, 80) + rnorm(.N, 0, 80 * sqrt(0.70)), 1)]
phe[, bf  := round(12 - 0.5 * (sex == "M") + bv(b_bf, 0.40, 2) + rnorm(.N, 0, 2 * sqrt(0.60)), 2)]
phe[, fcr := round(2.4 + bv(b_fcr, 0.25, 0.2) + rnorm(.N, 0, 0.2 * sqrt(0.75)), 3)]

# Missing phenotypes: an individual need not have all traits recorded
phe[sample(.N, 40), adg := NA]
phe[sample(.N, 60), bf  := NA]
phe[sample(.N, 30), fcr := NA]

phe
#>          id   herd    sex     batch    adg    bf   fcr
#>      <char> <char> <char>    <char>  <num> <num> <num>
#>   1:  N0001  north      F north2404  961.3    NA 2.268
#>   2:  N0002  north      F north2404  934.9 10.51 2.445
#>   3:  N0003  north      M north2403  918.7 10.74 2.690
#>   4:  N0004  north      F north2402  942.3 10.86    NA
#>   5:  N0005  north      M north2402 1071.9 14.88 2.259
#>  ---                                                  
#> 576:  S0276  south      F south2404  889.4 10.91 2.565
#> 577:  S0277  south      F south2401  983.7 10.06 2.317
#> 578:  S0278  south      F south2402     NA    NA 2.052
#> 579:  S0279  south      F south2404  957.4 10.71 2.396
#> 580:  S0280  south      F south2404  787.5 10.91 2.567
phe[, .N, by = herd]
#>      herd     N
#>    <char> <int>
#> 1:  north   300
#> 2:  south   280

With your own data, the phenotype table needs:

  • one row per individual (or several rows for repeated records, see the FAQ);
  • an ID column whose IDs match the genotype file / G matrix;
  • a grouping column (population, herd, line, …); each individual belongs to exactly one group.

Why all models should share one fold table

Two models are best compared on the same validation individuals. Otherwise their difference also contains the random error of validating different individuals, and comparing them fold by fold is meaningless.

Calling nest_cv() per trait gives each trait its own random split:

cv_old <- nest_cv(w2l_nest(phe, cols = c("adg", "bf"), by = "herd"), v = 5, seed = 1)
v_adg <- cv_old[name == "adg" & herd == "north" & id == "Fold1", validate[[1]]$id]
v_bf  <- cv_old[name == "bf"  & herd == "north" & id == "Fold1", validate[[1]]$id]
c(adg_fold1 = length(v_adg), both = length(intersect(v_adg, v_bf)))
#> adg_fold1      both 
#>        60        10

Both are called Fold1, but only 10 of the 60 adg validation individuals are also in the bf validation set. Comparing a single-trait adg model with an adg + bf model on such folds compares two different sets of animals.

cv_folds() instead splits the individuals once, and every trait and model takes its split from that table by ID.

Step 1: one fold table, cv_folds() 

folds <- cv_folds(phe, id = "id", by = "herd", v = 5, repeats = 10, seed = 123)
folds
#>         herd     id      rep   fold
#>       <char> <char>   <char> <char>
#>    1:  north  N0001 Repeat01  Fold4
#>    2:  north  N0002 Repeat01  Fold4
#>    3:  north  N0003 Repeat01  Fold5
#>    4:  north  N0004 Repeat01  Fold3
#>    5:  north  N0005 Repeat01  Fold4
#>   ---                              
#> 5796:  south  S0276 Repeat10  Fold1
#> 5797:  south  S0277 Repeat10  Fold5
#> 5798:  south  S0278 Repeat10  Fold5
#> 5799:  south  S0279 Repeat10  Fold2
#> 5800:  south  S0280 Repeat10  Fold1

Each row is “the fold in which an individual is validated in one repeat”:

  • herd: the grouping column; folds are built independently within each group;
  • id: the individual;
  • rep: the repeat (Repeat01 … Repeat10);
  • fold: the fold in which this individual is validated in this repeat (Fold1 … Fold5).

In every repeat each individual appears exactly once, and fold sizes differ by at most one:

folds[, .N, by = .(herd, rep, id)][, all(N == 1L)]
#> [1] TRUE
folds[rep == "Repeat01", .N, by = .(herd, fold)]
#>       herd   fold     N
#>     <char> <char> <int>
#>  1:  north  Fold4    60
#>  2:  north  Fold5    60
#>  3:  north  Fold3    60
#>  4:  north  Fold1    60
#>  5:  north  Fold2    60
#>  6:  south  Fold5    56
#>  7:  south  Fold1    56
#>  8:  south  Fold4    56
#>  9:  south  Fold3    56
#> 10:  south  Fold2    56

Repeats are independent random splits, so an individual moves between folds across repeats:

folds[id == "N0001", .(rep, fold)]
#>          rep   fold
#>       <char> <char>
#>  1: Repeat01  Fold4
#>  2: Repeat02  Fold1
#>  3: Repeat03  Fold3
#>  4: Repeat04  Fold3
#>  5: Repeat05  Fold1
#>  6: Repeat06  Fold5
#>  7: Repeat07  Fold3
#>  8: Repeat08  Fold1
#>  9: Repeat09  Fold4
#> 10: Repeat10  Fold5

Stratification

To spread a factor (e.g. sex) evenly over the folds, use strata. It must be constant within an individual; numeric columns are binned at quantiles first:

f_sex <- cv_folds(phe, id = "id", by = "herd", v = 5, strata = "sex", seed = 1)
dcast(f_sex[phe, on = "id", sex := i.sex][herd == "north"], sex ~ fold, value.var = "id", fun.aggregate = length)
#> Key: <sex>
#>       sex Fold1 Fold2 Fold3 Fold4 Fold5
#>    <char> <int> <int> <int> <int> <int>
#> 1:      F    27    28    27    28    27
#> 2:      M    33    32    33    32    33

Adding repeats later

Repeats are generated one after another, so with the same seed a larger repeats leaves the existing repeats unchanged, and results already computed can be kept:

f3 <- cv_folds(phe, id = "id", by = "herd", v = 5, repeats = 3, seed = 123)
identical(f3$fold, folds$fold[seq_len(nrow(f3))])
#> [1] TRUE

Only the label width changes when repeats goes from one to two digits (Repeat1 → Repeat01); the split does not.

Step 2: five scenarios, cv_scenarios() 

traits <- c("adg", "bf", "fcr")
sc <- cv_scenarios(phe, cols = traits, id = "id", group = "herd", folds = folds)
sc
#> <mintyr_scenarios> 580 individuals, 10 x 5
#>   st_sp  param:   6 data sets | cv:  300 train/validate pairs
#>   st_mp  param:   3 data sets | cv:  300 train/validate pairs
#>   mt_sp  param:   6 data sets | cv:  300 train/validate pairs
#>   mt_mp  param:   3 data sets | cv:  300 train/validate pairs
#>   mt_bt  param:   3 data sets | cv:  300 train/validate pairs

The five scenarios:

Scenario Model Parameter data Training set Validation set
st_sp single-trait, single group trait × group other folds of the target group current fold of the target group
st_mp single-trait, groups combined trait same + all records of the other groups same
mt_sp two-trait, single group trait pair × group other folds of the target group same
mt_mp two-trait, groups combined trait pair same + all records of the other groups same
mt_bt one trait treated as a different trait in each group (genetic correlation between groups) trait same + all records of the other groups same

Each scenario is a list with param (parameter-estimation data) and cv (cross-validation data).

Parameter-estimation data 

sc$st_sp$param     # single group: one data set per trait x group
#>      name   herd                data
#>    <char> <char>              <list>
#> 1:    adg  north <data.table[300x5]>
#> 2:    adg  south <data.table[280x5]>
#> 3:     bf  north <data.table[300x5]>
#> 4:     bf  south <data.table[280x5]>
#> 5:    fcr  north <data.table[300x5]>
#> 6:    fcr  south <data.table[280x5]>
sc$st_mp$param     # groups combined: one data set per trait
#>      name                data
#>    <char>              <list>
#> 1:    adg <data.table[580x5]>
#> 2:     bf <data.table[580x5]>
#> 3:    fcr <data.table[580x5]>
sc$mt_sp$param     # trait pair x group
#>      pairs   herd                data
#>     <char> <char>              <list>
#> 1:  adg-bf  north <data.table[300x6]>
#> 2:  adg-bf  south <data.table[280x6]>
#> 3: adg-fcr  north <data.table[300x6]>
#> 4: adg-fcr  south <data.table[280x6]>
#> 5:  bf-fcr  north <data.table[300x6]>
#> 6:  bf-fcr  south <data.table[280x6]>
head(sc$mt_sp$param$data[[1]])
#>        id   herd    sex     batch value1 value2
#>    <char> <char> <char>    <char>  <num>  <num>
#> 1:  N0001  north      F north2404  961.3     NA
#> 2:  N0002  north      F north2404  934.9  10.51
#> 3:  N0003  north      M north2403  918.7  10.74
#> 4:  N0004  north      F north2402  942.3  10.86
#> 5:  N0005  north      M north2402 1071.9  14.88
#> 6:  N0006  north      F north2404  873.7  11.46

In two-trait data the values are in value1 and value2, in the order of pairs (in adg-bf, value1 is adg). Rows with missing phenotypes are kept: an individual recorded for only one of the two traits is exactly the information a multi-trait model uses.

Cross-validation data 

sc$st_mp$cv
#>        name   herd      rep   fold               train           validate
#>      <char> <char>   <char> <char>              <list>             <list>
#>   1:    adg  north Repeat01  Fold1 <data.table[520x5]> <data.table[60x5]>
#>   2:    adg  north Repeat01  Fold2 <data.table[520x5]> <data.table[60x5]>
#>   3:    adg  north Repeat01  Fold3 <data.table[520x5]> <data.table[60x5]>
#>   4:    adg  north Repeat01  Fold4 <data.table[520x5]> <data.table[60x5]>
#>   5:    adg  north Repeat01  Fold5 <data.table[520x5]> <data.table[60x5]>
#>  ---                                                                     
#> 296:    fcr  south Repeat10  Fold1 <data.table[524x5]> <data.table[56x5]>
#> 297:    fcr  south Repeat10  Fold2 <data.table[524x5]> <data.table[56x5]>
#> 298:    fcr  south Repeat10  Fold3 <data.table[524x5]> <data.table[56x5]>
#> 299:    fcr  south Repeat10  Fold4 <data.table[524x5]> <data.table[56x5]>
#> 300:    fcr  south Repeat10  Fold5 <data.table[524x5]> <data.table[56x5]>

Each row is one trait (or pair) × validated group × repeat × fold, with the train and validate tables. In st_mp the training set holds all records of the other group, and the validation set comes from the target group only:

sc$st_mp$cv[1, .(
  name, herd, rep, fold,
  n_train          = nrow(train[[1]]),
  herds_in_train   = paste(unique(train[[1]]$herd), collapse = ", "),
  n_validate       = nrow(validate[[1]]),
  herd_in_validate = unique(validate[[1]]$herd)
)]
#>      name   herd      rep   fold n_train herds_in_train n_validate
#>    <char> <char>   <char> <char>   <int>         <char>      <int>
#> 1:    adg  north Repeat01  Fold1     520   north, south         60
#>    herd_in_validate
#>              <char>
#> 1:            north

All five scenarios validate the same individuals

This is what the shared fold table buys: for a given group × repeat × fold, every scenario and every trait validates the same individuals.

val_ids <- function(cv) {
  cv[, .(herd, rep, fold,
         ids = vapply(validate, function(d) paste(sort(d$id), collapse = ","), ""))]
}
all_v <- rbindlist(lapply(c("st_sp", "st_mp", "mt_sp", "mt_mp", "mt_bt"),
                          function(s) val_ids(sc[[s]]$cv)))
all_v[, uniqueN(ids), by = .(herd, rep, fold)][, all(V1 == 1L)]
#> [1] TRUE

One file layout

Every data set keeps all non-trait columns (including the group column herd) in their original order; only the trait columns differ. mt_bt spreads the trait into one column per group, an individual having a value only in its own group’s column, and training and validation sets have the same columns:

head(sc$mt_bt$cv$train[[1]], 3)
#>        id   herd    sex     batch north south
#>    <char> <char> <char>    <char> <num> <num>
#> 1:  N0001  north      F north2404 961.3    NA
#> 2:  N0002  north      F north2404 934.9    NA
#> 3:  N0003  north      M north2403 918.7    NA
names(sc$mt_bt$cv$validate[[1]])
#> [1] "id"    "herd"  "sex"   "batch" "north" "south"

To fit the group as a fixed effect (st_mp, mt_mp), use the herd column.

Only some scenarios 

sc2 <- cv_scenarios(phe, cols = traits, id = "id", group = "herd", folds = folds,
                    scenarios = c("st_sp", "mt_sp"))

Without folds, cv_scenarios() calls cv_folds() itself with v, repeats, strata and seed. Building the fold table first, as above, is still recommended: it is part of the result, needed to summarise accuracies and to add models later.

Step 3: write the files, export_scenarios() 

out <- file.path(tempdir(), "gblup")
files <- export_scenarios(
  sc,
  path = out,
  dirs = c(st_sp = "2.1.st_sp", st_mp = "2.2.st_mp", mt_sp = "2.3.mt_sp",
           mt_mp = "2.4.mt_mp", mt_bt = "2.5.mt_bt"),
  na   = "."
)
length(files)
#> [1] 3021
head(substring(files, nchar(out) + 2), 4)
#> [1] "2.1.st_sp/param_est_data/adg/north/data.txt"
#> [2] "2.1.st_sp/param_est_data/adg/south/data.txt"
#> [3] "2.1.st_sp/param_est_data/bf/north/data.txt" 
#> [4] "2.1.st_sp/param_est_data/bf/south/data.txt"
tail(substring(files, nchar(out) + 2), 2)
#> [1] "2.5.mt_bt/cv_data/fcr/south/Repeat10/Fold5/train.txt"   
#> [2] "2.5.mt_bt/cv_data/fcr/south/Repeat10/Fold5/validate.txt"

The layout is:

<path>/<scenario dir>/param_est_data/<trait or pair>[/<group>]/data.txt
<path>/<scenario dir>/cv_data/<trait or pair>/<group>/<repeat>/<fold>/train.txt
<path>/<scenario dir>/cv_data/<trait or pair>/<group>/<repeat>/<fold>/validate.txt
readLines(file.path(out, "2.5.mt_bt", "cv_data", "adg", "north", "Repeat01", "Fold1", "train.txt"), n = 3)
#> [1] "id\therd\tsex\tbatch\tnorth\tsouth"  
#> [2] "N0001\tnorth\tF\tnorth2404\t961.3\t."
#> [3] "N0002\tnorth\tF\tnorth2404\t934.9\t."

Save the fold table too; it is needed to summarise, reproduce or extend the analysis:

fwrite(folds, file.path(out, "cv_folds.txt"), sep = "\t")

Missing values and headers for each program

na sets the missing-value code; other arguments (e.g. col.names) are passed to data.table::fwrite():

Program Typical call
ASReml (standalone) na = "." (NA and * also work)
HIBLUP na = "NA"
DMU na = "-9999", col.names = FALSE, and all columns numeric 
export_scenarios(sc, path = "dmu_runs", na = "-9999", col.names = FALSE)

DMU needs integer codes for class variables and IDs. Add coded columns before cv_scenarios(); the ID codes must match those of the pedigree / genotype files.

Step 4: summarise prediction accuracy

Once the models have run, compute accuracies per scenario × trait × group × repeat × fold. To keep this article runnable, a simplified SNP-BLUP (ridge regression, equivalent to GBLUP under the same assumptions) stands in for the external program: fixed effects are removed with lm(), SNP effects are estimated on the training set, and the GEBVs of the validation individuals are correlated with their corrected phenotypes.

snp_blup_r <- function(tr, va, h2) {
  tr  <- tr[!is.na(value)]
  va  <- va[!is.na(value)]
  fe  <- lm(value ~ sex + batch, data = tr)            # fixed effects (batch includes herd)
  Zt  <- Z[tr$id, , drop = FALSE]
  lam <- sum(2 * freq * (1 - freq)) * (1 - h2) / h2
  b   <- solve(crossprod(Zt) + diag(lam, ncol(Zt)), crossprod(Zt, residuals(fe)))
  gebv <- drop(Z[va$id, , drop = FALSE] %*% b)
  cor(gebv, va$value - predict(fe, va))
}
h2 <- c(adg = 0.30, bf = 0.40, fcr = 0.25)

fold_r <- function(cv) {
  cv <- copy(cv)
  cv[, r := mapply(snp_blup_r, train, validate, h2[name])]
  cv[, .(name, herd, rep, fold, r)]
}
res <- rbind(fold_r(sc$st_sp$cv)[, scenario := "st_sp"],
             fold_r(sc$st_mp$cv)[, scenario := "st_mp"])
head(res)
#>      name   herd      rep   fold         r scenario
#>    <char> <char>   <char> <char>     <num>   <char>
#> 1:    adg  north Repeat01  Fold1 0.4220073    st_sp
#> 2:    adg  north Repeat01  Fold2 0.1312988    st_sp
#> 3:    adg  north Repeat01  Fold3 0.2962800    st_sp
#> 4:    adg  north Repeat01  Fold4 0.1342538    st_sp
#> 5:    adg  north Repeat01  Fold5 0.2680499    st_sp
#> 6:    adg  north Repeat02  Fold1 0.2116165    st_sp

With an external program, replace snp_blup_r() by reading its GEBV output from each folder, for example:

cv <- copy(sc$st_sp$cv)
cv[, dir := file.path(out, "2.1.st_sp", "cv_data", name, herd, rep, fold)]
cv[, r := mapply(function(d, va) {
  g <- fread(file.path(d, "gebv.txt"))          # assumed columns: id, gebv
  m <- merge(va, g, by = "id")
  cor(m$gebv, m$value, use = "complete.obs")    # often divided by sqrt(h2)
}, dir, validate)]

Average within repeats, then compare models

Folds of one repeat share most of their training individuals and are not independent. Average the folds within each repeat first, then report mean ± SD over repeats:

by_rep <- res[, .(r = mean(r)), by = .(scenario, name, herd, rep)]
by_rep[, .(mean_r = mean(r), sd_r = sd(r)), by = .(scenario, name, herd)]
#>     scenario   name   herd    mean_r       sd_r
#>       <char> <char> <char>     <num>      <num>
#>  1:    st_sp    adg  north 0.2245990 0.03348924
#>  2:    st_sp    adg  south 0.2636457 0.02764120
#>  3:    st_sp     bf  north 0.2999839 0.03717908
#>  4:    st_sp     bf  south 0.1419841 0.03052602
#>  5:    st_sp    fcr  north 0.1355088 0.04063370
#>  6:    st_sp    fcr  south 0.1448240 0.03110184
#>  7:    st_mp    adg  north 0.2242383 0.02390440
#>  8:    st_mp    adg  south 0.2176988 0.02433537
#>  9:    st_mp     bf  north 0.4221658 0.02351719
#> 10:    st_mp     bf  south 0.3358666 0.02305682
#> 11:    st_mp    fcr  north 0.1942041 0.02982955
#> 12:    st_mp    fcr  south 0.1973909 0.02034039

Compare two models paired by repeat, testing the repeat-level differences:

paired <- dcast(by_rep, name + herd + rep ~ scenario, value.var = "r")
paired[, d := st_mp - st_sp]
paired[, .(mean_diff = mean(d), se = sd(d) / sqrt(.N), p = t.test(d)$p.value),
       by = .(name, herd)]
#> Key: <name, herd>
#>      name   herd     mean_diff          se            p
#>    <char> <char>         <num>       <num>        <num>
#> 1:    adg  north -0.0003607033 0.005797351 9.517486e-01
#> 2:    adg  south -0.0459468926 0.003230831 1.790677e-07
#> 3:     bf  north  0.1221818801 0.005950163 7.195172e-09
#> 4:     bf  south  0.1938825428 0.007464497 8.963559e-10
#> 5:    fcr  north  0.0586952944 0.005278115 1.468514e-06
#> 6:    fcr  south  0.0525669380 0.005387039 4.385782e-06

This pairing is valid only because all scenarios validate the same individuals.

In these simulated data, adding the other herd clearly improves bf and fcr, but not adg. Different conclusions for different traits of the same data are common in practice too, so report results per trait and per group rather than one overall average. Accuracies are often reported as the correlation divided by h2\sqrt{h^2}.

Beyond the five scenarios

cv_scenarios() covers the five most common scenarios. Other designs can be built with apply_folds() and the same fold table, still validating the same individuals as above.

Three-trait models 

mt3 <- apply_folds(c2p_nest(phe, cols = traits, pairs_n = 3), folds, ref = "others")
mt3[1:2]
#>         pairs   herd      rep   fold               train           validate
#>        <char> <char>   <char> <char>              <list>             <list>
#> 1: adg-bf-fcr  north Repeat01  Fold1 <data.table[520x7]> <data.table[60x7]>
#> 2: adg-bf-fcr  north Repeat01  Fold2 <data.table[520x7]> <data.table[60x7]>
names(mt3$train[[1]])
#> [1] "id"     "herd"   "sex"    "batch"  "value1" "value2" "value3"

Some traits or some groups only 

cv_adg_north <- apply_folds(w2l_nest(phe[herd == "north"], cols = "adg"), folds)
nrow(cv_adg_north)
#> [1] 50

Groups of the fold table that do not occur in the data are skipped; individuals in the data but not in the fold table are dropped with a warning.

Masking: one file, validation phenotypes set to missing

Some programs prefer one complete data set in which the phenotypes of the validation individuals are set to missing. Combine training and validation sets into one file:

cv <- copy(sc$st_sp$cv)
cv[, masked := Map(function(tr, va) rbind(tr, copy(va)[, value := NA]), train, validate)]
cv$masked[[1]][, .(n = .N, n_missing = sum(is.na(value)))]
#>        n n_missing
#>    <int>     <int>
#> 1:   300        75
export_nest(cv, by = c("name", "herd", "rep", "fold"), cols = "masked",
            path = "masked_runs", na = ".")

For two-trait data, set both value1 and value2 to missing.

Across-group prediction: one group predicts another

Training on the south herd only and predicting the north herd needs no folds:

across <- w2l_nest(phe, cols = traits)[, .(
  train    = lapply(data, function(d) d[herd == "south"]),
  validate = lapply(data, function(d) d[herd == "north"])
), by = name]
across
#>      name               train            validate
#>    <char>              <list>              <list>
#> 1:    adg <data.table[280x5]> <data.table[300x5]>
#> 2:     bf <data.table[280x5]> <data.table[300x5]>
#> 3:    fcr <data.table[280x5]> <data.table[300x5]>

The genotypes of both groups must then be in one G matrix.

ASReml-R inside R

out_type = "df" returns every subset as a data.frame, ready for asreml():

sc_df <- cv_scenarios(phe, cols = traits, id = "id", group = "herd",
                      folds = folds, scenarios = "st_sp", out_type = "df")
cv <- sc_df$st_sp$cv
cv[, r := mapply(function(tr, va) {
  tr$id <- factor(tr$id, levels = rownames(Ginv))
  fit <- asreml::asreml(value ~ sex + batch, random = ~ vm(id, Ginv),
                        data = tr, na.action = asreml::na.method(y = "include"))
  gebv <- predict(fit, classify = "id")$pvals
  m <- merge(va, gebv, by = "id")
  cor(m$predicted.value, m$value, use = "complete.obs")
}, train, validate)]

FAQ

What is required of the IDs? An ID may belong to one group only; otherwise cv_folds() stops and lists those IDs. IDs must match the genotype file. Individuals without genotypes cannot be predicted by GBLUP, so drop them from the phenotypes before building the fold table (single-step ssGBLUP aside).

Repeated records (several rows per individual)? They are fine. cv_folds() splits individuals, so all records of an individual are always in the same fold: no information leaks from training to validation through other records of the same animal.

Are rows with missing phenotypes removed? No. All scenarios keep them, and they are written with the na code. When computing accuracies, use use = "complete.obs" or drop validation individuals without a phenotype.

Why rep / fold instead of id / id2 as in nest_cv()? Because the individual ID column is often called id itself. The exported folders are still named Repeat01/Fold1.

How do I reproduce the same split later? Pass seed to cv_folds(); it affects only this split and leaves the random-number stream of the rest of your script alone. Also save the fold table to a file.

Can I build the fold table now and add models later? Yes, that is the recommended workflow. Any new model built with the same fold table, through apply_folds() or cv_scenarios(folds = folds), validates the same individuals as all earlier models.
